passages.title: The Benefits of Learning English
passages.content:
English is one of the most widely spoken languages in the world. More than 1.5 billion people speak English, either as their first or second language. Learning English can open many doors for you in life.

First, English is the language of international business. Many multinational companies require their employees to speak English. If you can communicate effectively in English, you will have a significant advantage in the job market.

Second, most scientific research and academic papers are published in English. Students who can read English have access to a much wider range of educational resources.

Third, English is the primary language of the internet. A large percentage of websites, videos, and online content are in English.

Finally, learning English can help you understand different cultures and connect with people from all over the world.

passages.title: The Return of the Urban Beekeeper
passages.content:
A
Twenty years ago, the idea of keeping bees on the roof of an office building would have struck most city planners as eccentric at best. Bees belonged to the countryside, to orchards and wildflower meadows, not to car parks and shopping streets. Today, however, hives can be found on hotels in Paris, railway stations in Tokyo and apartment blocks in Melbourne. In London alone, the number of registered hives more than doubled between 2008 and 2013.

B
The trend began partly as a response to alarming news from the countryside. From the mid-2000s, beekeepers in North America and Europe reported losing large proportions of their colonies over the winter, a problem that became known as colony collapse. Pesticides, parasites and a shrinking variety of flowers on industrial farms were all blamed. Many people concluded that cities, with their parks and private gardens, might offer bees a safer home.

C
There is some evidence to support this view. Because urban gardeners plant a wide range of ornamental species, flowers are available in cities for much of the year, and pesticide use in private gardens is often lower than on farms. A study of honey produced in Paris found that it contained pollen from more than two hundred plant species, compared with around fifty in honey from nearby farmland. City bees, in other words, may enjoy a more varied diet.

D
Yet ecologists warn that enthusiasm has outrun the evidence. The honeybee is only one of thousands of bee species, and most of the others are wild and solitary, nesting in the ground or in hollow stems. These wild bees are the ones in serious decline, and they compete with honeybees for the same nectar and pollen. Where hives are packed too densely, as in parts of central London, there may simply not be enough flowers to go around. Researchers in that city calculated that some districts would need several times more green space to support the colonies already registered there.

E
For this reason, several cities have begun to change their approach. Rather than encouraging every company to install a hive as a sign of its environmental credentials, they now promote 'pollinator corridors': connected strips of flowering plants along roads, railways and rivers. These corridors benefit all kinds of insects, not only honeybees, and they are cheaper to maintain than hives, which need regular inspection by a trained keeper.

F
None of this means that urban beekeeping should disappear. Hives on school roofs have proved to be a powerful teaching tool, giving children who rarely see the countryside a direct experience of how food is produced. The lesson for city authorities is one of balance: a few well-managed hives, surrounded by plenty of flowers, can do more good than hundreds of hives competing for a handful of window boxes.

passages.title: Sleep and the Teenage Brain
passages.content:
Parents have long complained that teenagers stay up too late and are impossible to wake in the morning. For most of the twentieth century this was treated as a matter of discipline: adolescents, it was assumed, simply lacked the self-control to go to bed. Research over the last three decades suggests a different explanation. The timing of sleep, it turns out, is governed by a biological clock that shifts significantly during the teenage years.

The key to this clock is melatonin, a hormone released in the evening that makes us feel drowsy. In children and adults, melatonin levels typically begin to rise around nine or ten o'clock at night. In adolescents, the release is delayed by as much as two hours. A sixteen-year-old who is sent to bed at ten may therefore lie awake for a long time, not out of defiance but because the body is not yet ready for sleep. The same delay means that waking at six-thirty feels, to a teenager, much as waking at four-thirty would feel to an adult.

This would matter less if teenagers needed less sleep than adults, but the opposite is true. Most studies estimate that adolescents require between eight and a half and nine and a half hours a night. Surveys in several countries have found that the majority get fewer than seven on school nights. The consequences go beyond tiredness. Sleep-deprived students perform worse on tests of memory and attention, and they are more likely to report low mood. Some researchers have also linked short sleep to a higher risk of road accidents among young drivers.

One response has been to start the school day later. When a group of schools in the American state of Minnesota moved their opening time from 7.15 to 8.40 in the 1990s, researchers found that students slept almost an hour more each night, attendance improved and fewer students fell asleep in class. Similar results have since been reported elsewhere. Critics point out that later starts can be expensive, because bus timetables and after-school sports must be reorganised, and that parents who work early may struggle with the change. In my view, however, these practical difficulties are a weak argument against a policy whose benefits are so well documented.

Not every problem can be blamed on biology. Screens, in particular, make the situation worse: the blue light from phones and tablets suppresses melatonin further, and messages arriving late at night keep the brain alert. Yet it would be a mistake to assume that removing phones from bedrooms would solve the problem on its own. Even teenagers who follow good sleep habits are fighting against their internal clock when they are expected at school before eight.

What the research offers, ultimately, is a change of attitude. A tired adolescent is not necessarily a lazy one. If schools and families accept that the teenage body runs on a different timetable, they can design days that work with that timetable rather than against it.

passages.title: Reviving Silent Tongues
passages.content:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that around forty per cent are endangered, meaning that they are no longer being learned by children as a first language. When the last fluent speaker of such a language dies, a unique way of describing the world disappears with them. Yet the story is not only one of loss. Over the past fifty years, a growing number of communities have attempted to bring their languages back into everyday use, and some of these efforts have been remarkably successful.

The best-known example is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly for religious and scholarly purposes. In the late nineteenth century, a small group of enthusiasts began to speak it at home and to create new words for modern objects. Within two generations it had become the first language of millions. Linguist Ghil'ad Zuckermann has argued, however, that the language spoken today is not simply the Hebrew of ancient texts brought back to life; it is a new language, shaped strongly by the European languages its first modern speakers already knew. In his view, every revived language is to some extent a hybrid.

A very different approach was taken in New Zealand, where in the early 1980s Maori elders, concerned that few young families could speak their ancestral language, set up 'language nests'. In these pre-school centres, children spend the whole day with fluent older speakers and hear no English at all. The model spread quickly, and primary and secondary schools teaching entirely through Maori followed. Sociolinguist Bernard Spolsky observed that the nests succeeded because they involved parents and grandparents as well as children, turning language learning into a family activity rather than a school subject.

In Wales, the emphasis has been on official status. Since the 1990s, Welsh has had equal standing with English in public life, and road signs, government forms and a television channel all use it. Researcher Colin Williams has cautioned, though, that visibility is not the same as use. A language may appear on every sign and still be spoken at home by a shrinking minority, and he has argued that what matters most is whether young people choose to use it with their friends.

Technology has opened another route. Communities with only a handful of speakers now record elders telling stories, build online dictionaries and develop learning apps. Linguist Margaret Florey, who has worked with communities in eastern Indonesia, notes that recordings are valuable but warns against treating them as a substitute for speakers. A dictionary, she points out, can preserve a language's words, but only a community can keep it alive.

What do successful projects have in common? Most researchers agree on three conditions. First, the community itself must want the language back; programmes imposed from outside rarely last. Second, children must hear the language early and often, ideally at home. Third, the language needs spaces in modern life, from shops to social media, where using it feels natural rather than ceremonial. Revival, it seems, is less a technical problem than a social one, and it depends above all on ordinary people deciding to speak.

passages.title: A Saturday Market
passages.content:
A
Every Saturday, the old bus station in Riverside becomes a market. It opens at seven in the morning and closes at one. About eighty stalls stand in three rows. The first row sells fruit and vegetables. The second row sells bread, cheese and cooked food. The third row sells clothes, books and household goods. Entry is free, but the car park beside the station costs 10,000 dong an hour.

B
Mai has had a fruit stall there for six years. She arrives at half past five to unload boxes of oranges, mangoes and herbs. Her prices are written on a small board: oranges are 25,000 dong a kilo, and mangoes are 40,000. She keeps a tin for change under the table and does not take cards. On a busy morning she sells about thirty kilos of fruit. Her brother helps her after nine, when he finishes his shift at the bakery next door.

C
The market also has a notice board near the gate. This week it says that next Saturday the third row will close because the council is repairing the roof. Clothes and books will move to the school playground across the road for that one day. Cooked food will stay in the second row, but hot drinks will stop at noon instead of one. Visitors who want a table should come before eleven, because the six shared tables fill up quickly.

passages.title: The School Garden Project
passages.content:
In 2019, Westfield Secondary School turned an unused corner of its playground into a garden. The head teacher, Helen Ward, wanted students to learn where food comes from, and she also hoped the garden would give them a reason to spend time outdoors. A local nursery donated soil, seeds and twenty wooden beds. Parents built the beds over one weekend.

The garden now has three parts. The sunny beds grow tomatoes, beans and herbs. A shaded bed is used for lettuce. Behind them, a small shed stores tools and a rainwater tank. Students in Years 7 and 8 look after the plants on a rota: each class has the garden for one lesson a week. They record the temperature, the amount of water used, and which plants are ready to pick.

The project has changed more than the playground. In a survey of 140 students in 2023, 68% said they had tried a vegetable at school that they had never eaten at home. Science teachers use the records in lessons on measurement and plant growth. The school kitchen takes herbs and tomatoes twice a week during term, which has cut a small part of the vegetable bill.

There have been problems. During the long holiday the beds dried out, and in 2021 a storm broke the shed roof. The school now pays a neighbour, Mr Cole, a small fee to water the beds in July. Students also found that lettuce failed when it was planted in full sun, so they moved it. Ward says the garden is not meant to feed the whole school. Its value is that students plan, measure, fail and try again.

passages.title: A simple home water filter
passages.content:
Many homes now fit a small filter under the kitchen sink. The aim is to remove dirt and the taste of chlorine before water is used for drinking and cooking. The unit in the diagram has four parts, and water moves through them from left to right.

Tap water first enters the unit at point 1. It is still ordinary cold water from the mains. At point 2 it meets a fine screen. The screen catches sand and rust but does not change the taste. At point 3 the water passes through a block of carbon. The carbon holds on to chlorine and some of the smells that people notice in tap water. Finally, at point 4, the cleaned water comes out of a separate drinking tap beside the sink. Water used for washing dishes does not go through the filter.

The screen should be rinsed once a month. The carbon block lasts about six months in a family of four, and then it must be replaced. The filter does not make seawater drinkable, and it does not remove all bacteria. If the local supply is unsafe, the water should still be boiled.

passages.title: Repair cafes and the right to fix
passages.content:
On a wet Saturday in Bristol, a queue forms outside a church hall. People are not waiting for a concert. They are carrying toasters, lamps and a laptop that will not charge. Inside, volunteers with screwdrivers sit at long tables. This is a repair cafe, a place where neighbours help each other mend things instead of throwing them away.

The first repair cafe opened in Amsterdam in 2009. The idea spread quickly. Organisers say there are now thousands of similar events across Europe, North America and parts of Asia. Most are free. Visitors pay nothing for the labour, though they are often asked to bring a small donation for tea and spare parts. The point is not to replace professional shops. It is to keep simple objects in use for a few more years, and to show people that a broken switch is not always the end of a machine.

Researchers who have watched these events argue that the environmental gain is real but easy to overstate. A repaired kettle saves the energy and materials that would have gone into a new one. It does not, however, cancel the impact of the much larger things people buy, such as cars and heating systems. One Dutch study of repair cafes found that about two thirds of the items brought in were fixed on the day. The rest needed a part that nobody had, or were too badly damaged. Even the failures taught something: visitors left knowing why the object had died.

A harder problem is design. Many modern products are glued shut, or use screws that ordinary tools cannot turn. Campaigners call this the "right to fix". They want manufacturers to sell spare parts and to publish basic repair guides. Some governments have started to listen. France now requires a repair score on certain appliances, a number that tells shoppers how easy a product is to mend. Critics say the score is still too narrow, because it ignores how long software updates will last.

The volunteers in Bristol are more practical than political. A retired electrician shows a student how to test a fuse. A teenager leaves with a lamp that works and a small notebook of what she did. The cafe will be back next month. The queue, the organisers expect, will be just as long.

passages.title: Tiny forests in crowded cities
passages.content:
A patch of land the size of a tennis court does not look like a forest. Yet in cities from Tokyo to Utrecht, planners are planting dense groups of native trees and shrubs and calling them tiny forests. The method was popularised by the Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki, who argued that a carefully chosen mix of local species, planted close together, can form a stable woodland much faster than a conventional park plantation.

The appeal for city councils is obvious. A tiny forest fits into a schoolyard, a roadside verge or the corner of a car park. Within a few years the young trees shade the soil, and the leaf litter begins to hold water after heavy rain. Teachers use the plots for biology lessons. Residents say the sites are cooler in summer than the surrounding pavement. Birds and insects arrive before the trees are tall, because the planting includes flowers and berry shrubs as well as canopy species.

Evidence for the wider claims is still uneven. Supporters sometimes say a tiny forest absorbs as much carbon as a mature woodland of the same size. Forest scientists treat that comparison with caution. Young trees do grow quickly, but most of the carbon in an old forest sits in the soil and in large trunks, which a ten-year-old plot has not yet produced. A review of urban planting projects in the Netherlands found clear gains in shade and in the number of plant species. It found only modest, hard-to-measure changes in city-wide air temperature.

There are practical limits too. The Miyawaki method asks for deep soil preparation and a high number of seedlings, so the cost per square metre is higher than scattering a few street trees. If the species are poorly chosen, the thick planting becomes a thicket that neighbours dislike, and the council must pay to thin it. Watering is essential in the first two summers. After that, advocates say, the plot should survive with little care. Councils that skip the early watering often lose the very trees the brochure promised.

None of this makes the idea worthless. In a city that cannot spare a large park, a small native woodland is better than another sealed car park. The honest case is local: shade, habitat, a place for children to learn the names of trees. It is not a substitute for protecting existing forests outside the city.

passages.title: The cost of working at night
passages.content:
Hospitals, ports and bakeries do not close when the sun goes down. Someone has to staff them. In wealthy countries, roughly one worker in five sometimes works a night shift. The arrangement keeps services running, but a growing body of research suggests it carries a health cost that rotas rarely show.

The human body clock expects sleep in the dark and food during the day. Night work pushes against both habits. People who finish a shift at dawn often sleep in short blocks, and the sleep they get is lighter. Over months, that shortage is linked with higher rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes and some cardiovascular disease. The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classed night shift work as probably carcinogenic, mainly because of the long-term disruption of circadian rhythms, not because of one bad week.

Not every night worker is affected in the same way. Dr Helen Okonkwo, who studies hospital staff in Lagos, points out that nurses with some control over their rota report less fatigue than those whose shifts are imposed at short notice. A second line of research, led by the chronobiologist Marco Rossi in Milan, finds that people he calls "night types", who naturally stay up late, adapt a little better than strong morning types. Adaptation is only partial. Even night types still show disturbed glucose control after a run of night shifts.

Employers have tried several fixes. Bright light during the shift and very dark bedrooms afterwards help some people move their clock. Short naps of about twenty minutes, taken before 4 a.m., improve alertness without making it harder to sleep later. What does not work, according to a review by the occupational physician Samuel Berg, is simply telling staff to "catch up at the weekend". Two long lie-ins do not repay five short sleeps, and the Monday return to nights becomes harder, not easier.

Berg argues that the honest response is to treat night work as a limited resource. He recommends capping long runs of nights, publishing rotas at least two weeks ahead, and paying a real premium rather than a token one. Okonkwo agrees about notice periods but is wary of bans: in a city with too few nurses, a ban on nights would close wards. Vescovi, for his part, wants shift design to start from biology, with the heaviest tasks placed earlier in the night when attention is higher. None of them claims that a perfect rota exists. They claim that a careless one is a choice.

passages.title: Four views on city trees
passages.content:
A recent seminar brought together four researchers who disagree about how cities should plant trees.
Dr Lena Ortiz measured air temperature on two narrow streets that were alike in every way except shade. On the street with a continuous line of trees, the afternoon reading was three degrees lower. She argues that this cooling is the clearest benefit cities can expect, and that wide avenues already have enough breeze to need fewer trees.
Professor Hasan Malik looked at repair records rather than temperature. Where roots had been planted within two metres of old clay drains, the pipes cracked within a decade. He does not oppose trees, but he insists that the planting line must stay clear of ageing pipes.
Dr Mei Chen followed forty newly planted trees through their first summer. The ones that survived were not those nearest a tap. They were the ones on blocks where a single neighbour had agreed to water them twice a week and to remind the others. Without that person, even well-sited trees dried out.
Professor Owen Blake is less interested in how many species a park contains. He tracked small birds and found that they rarely crossed a busy road unless a line of trees or shrubs joined one green space to the next. A long list of species inside one isolated park, he says, does less for those birds than a plain corridor between parks.

passages.content:
Leaf blowers have become a regular part of city maintenance, and the present free-for-all is a mistake. Crews use the machines at all hours, including Sunday mornings, when the noise carries straight into bedrooms.
